opus-5.5.text:
I think the way to see it is that pre-training gives you an incredibly rich prior. These models have read basically everything humans have written, so they've absorbed a lot of the patterns of reasoning. But imitation only takes you so far. When you train on human data, you're learning to produce text that looks like what a person would write. You're not learning to actually solve the problem, and you're certainly not learning to go beyond the people whose data you trained on.

Reinforcement learning changes the objective. Instead of "predict the next token the way a human would," it's "find whatever sequence of steps actually gets you to the right answer." That's a fundamentally different signal. The model gets to try things, make mistakes, backtrack, and get rewarded when it succeeds. Over time it discovers strategies on its own: checking its work, decomposing a problem, trying another approach when the first one fails. Many of those behaviors aren't well represented in the training data, because people don't usually write down their messy internal search. They write down the clean final answer.

We saw this very clearly with AlphaGo and then AlphaZero. Supervised learning on human games got you a strong player, but the real leap came from self-play and RL, where the system could explore and find moves no human would have played, like move 37. I think reasoning in language models is in a similar place. Pre-training gets you to a competent starting point, and RL is what lets you climb past it, because the model is optimizing directly for outcomes rather than for resemblance to human text.

There's also a scaling argument. Human-written data is finite, and high-quality reasoning traces are even rarer. With RL, especially in domains where you can verify the answer, like math or code, the model is effectively generating its own training data. You can keep spending compute and keep getting better. That's a much more sustainable path to improvement than hoping someone writes more good proofs on the internet.

So for me, RL isn't just a nice add-on. It's the mechanism that turns a model that knows a lot into a model that can actually think through problems it hasn't seen before.

r001.rationale: The response says detailed reasoning traces are rare because people tend to publish clean final answers rather than their messy search, and notes the scarcity of human-written reasoning data.

r002.rationale: It explains that the model can try steps, make mistakes, and backtrack, then receive rewards for success; it also mentions verifying answers in domains such as math and code.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the simplest way to put it is that supervised learning can only take you as far as the data you already have. When you train a language model on human text, you're teaching it to imitate. And imitation is a very powerful thing, it gets you remarkably far, but it has a ceiling. The ceiling is the quality of the demonstrations. You can't really exceed the humans who wrote the data, because the objective is to match them, not to do better than them.

Reasoning is different from most of what's in a text corpus. When a person writes down a proof or works through a hard problem, what ends up on the page is usually the cleaned-up final version. The false starts, the backtracking, the "wait, that doesn't work, let me try something else" mostly don't get written down. So the model sees the answer, but it rarely sees the process that produced the answer. And if you want a model to actually reason rather than recall, it's the process that matters.

That's where reinforcement learning comes in. With RL, you stop asking "does this look like what a human wrote?" and start asking "did this actually work?" You give the model a problem where you can verify the outcome, a math problem, a piece of code with tests, something with a checkable answer, and you let it try. When it succeeds, you reinforce whatever it did to get there. When it fails, you don't. Over time the model discovers its own strategies for getting to correct answers, including strategies that no human demonstrated. It learns to check its work, to break things down, to recover from mistakes, because those behaviors get rewarded.

This is really the same lesson we learned with games. In the early AlphaGo work, we started by imitating human experts, and that got us to a strong amateur level. The jump to superhuman came from self-play, from the system learning from its own experience against a ground truth, the outcome of the game. AlphaZero made the point even more sharply: throw away the human data entirely and you still get there, in some ways better. The signal from "did I win or lose" turned out to be far more powerful than the signal from "did I play like a human."

Language models are messier because the world is not a board game, and for many tasks there's no clean win condition. But for reasoning specifically, there often is one. You can check whether the answer is right. And once you have a verifiable reward, you have the ingredients for the same kind of loop that worked in games: generate, evaluate, improve, repeat.

So I'd say RL is necessary not because supervised learning is bad, it's an excellent starting point, but because it's fundamentally bounded by its data. If you want a model to go past what it was shown, you need it to learn from consequences rather than from examples. That's what reinforcement learning is.

r001.rationale: The candidate says text corpora usually contain cleaned-up answers, while false starts and reasoning processes are rarely written down, limiting what imitation can teach.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes letting the model try verifiable problems and reinforcing successful attempts based on whether they produce correct answers.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that reasoning is something you learn by doing. Pretraining gives a model a very strong starting point: it learns from the reasoning that people have written down. But if you want it to discover better ways of solving problems, you need to let it attempt a solution and get feedback on whether it worked.

Reinforcement learning provides that loop. Take a math problem: the model can try different approaches, and if we can check the answer, we can reinforce the approaches that lead to success. We don’t necessarily have to tell it every step it should take. It can learn which steps are useful, when to reconsider an assumption, and when to spend more effort.

That’s why I see it as such an important ingredient. You move from learning from existing examples to learning from the consequences of your own attempts. And that opens up the possibility of discovering strategies that weren’t explicitly demonstrated in the training data.

r001.rationale: The response says pretraining learns from written reasoning, but does not identify a scarcity of detailed reasoning examples in internet data as a limitation.

r002.rationale: It explains that the model can attempt solutions, receive feedback on whether they worked, and reinforce successful approaches.

sol-6.1.text:
I think reinforcement learning is important because there’s a difference between learning to imitate a good answer and learning how to arrive at one. When you train a language model to predict the next token, it learns from the reasoning that appears in its training data. That gives you a very powerful starting point, but the training signal is still about predicting what somebody wrote.

With reinforcement learning, you can let the model try to solve a problem and give it feedback on whether it succeeded. If you can verify the answer, as you often can in mathematics or programming, the model can explore different approaches and learn which ones work. Potentially, it can discover strategies that aren’t demonstrated in the training data.

I wouldn’t say reinforcement learning is the only way to improve reasoning. But it gives us a way to move beyond imitation and learn directly from the consequences of the model’s own attempts.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts imitation with learning from attempts, but it does not identify a scarcity of detailed reasoning examples in internet data.

r002.rationale: It explains that the model can try to solve problems, receive feedback on whether it succeeded, and learn which approaches work from its own attempts.
